title: Sedation lightens — orient, pain, stop-on-signal
openingNarrative: Sedation is being reduced with a defined review reason: restore communication access, not make the room quieter. Rohan wakes fragmented. He may believe the bed is still moving—ambulance memories without relocating the arrest to the library. A ventilator alarm sounds once. The clinician identifies the ICU, confirms the airway is open and breaths are delivered, restores yes/no via cheek switch, asks about pain, and stops when Rohan signals stop. Reaching toward tubing is checked as pain or position first—not assumed line-pulling. Restraint is minimised. Samira’s fear about unnoticed emergencies is acknowledged; continuous bedroom-style video is not reintroduced as comfort.
clinicalState: Planned sedation reduction. Fluctuating delirium risk. Pain undetermined until asked accessibly. Communication method restored stepwise. Cardiac and respiratory domains carry forward branch consequences. No exact drug names or doses.

choices.label: Orient to ICU, restore yes/no, check pain, honour stop signal, avoid restraint
choices.immediateConsequence: Communication access rises; delirium burden eases modestly; restraint exposure stays low. Pain control improves if pain was present. Family burden falls because staff—not parents—run the access protocol.
choices.delayedConsequence: Delirium may continue in fragments; do not treat ongoing confusion as permanent incapacity. Privacy protection holds if telemetry stays proportionate.

choices.label: Keep deeper sedation a little longer to protect synchrony, with a written review time
choices.immediateConsequence: Ventilator synchrony may look smoother; communication access stays suppressed; delirium and authorship risk rise if the review time slips.
choices.delayedConsequence: Deep sedation must keep a clinical reason and review point—not convenience. Delayed harm: missed pain and lost consent windows.

choices.label: Rapid wake to maximise AAC immediately, accepting short-term distress risk
choices.immediateConsequence: Communication access jumps; distress and arrhythmia risk may rise; pain may be reported sooner if the method is ready.
choices.delayedConsequence: Rapid wake without orientation can intensify delirium fragments. Stop-on-signal still applies; do not flood with questions.
choices.rohanAacLine: NOW ASK ME WHAT HAPPENS NEXT.

disabilityRightsNotes: Deep sedation needs a clinical reason and review point—not room convenience.
Reaching may be communication; check pain and tubing before restraint.
Interrupted or slow AAC is not incapacity.
Do not reintroduce disproportionate video surveillance to soothe family fear.
debriefNotes: Prompt 6 audio wake scene pairs with this node.
Stop-on-signal is a rights-preserving control, not optional courtesy.
Ambulance memory fragments must not rewrite locked chronology.

accessibility.audioDescription: Narrator locates ICU daylight; clinician at eye level; cheek switch restored; one brief alarm with visual equivalent.
accessibility.reducedSensoryAlt: Reduced-sensory mix omits alarm audio; uses on-screen alarm banner and calmer ambience only.
